snip.t: A child from a malaria‑endemic area is comatose, with a peripheral smear showing *Plasmodium falciparum* parasites.
Distributive: Vasodilation and capillary leak — Severe bacterial sepsis, severe *Plasmodium falciparum* malaria, advanced HIV with cryptococcosis, anaphylaxis
The blood slide confirms heavy *Plasmodium falciparum* parasitaemia.
Thin film confirms severe *Plasmodium falciparum* malaria.

Severe malaria: Infection with asexual forms of *Plasmodium falciparum* (or rarely *P. vivax* / *P. knowlesi*) accompanied by one or more manifestations of acute, severe organ dysfunction, metabolic derangement, or hyperparasitemia.
*Plasmodium falciparum:* Responsible for >95% of infections and virtually all severe disease, complications, and mortality in Kenya.
Cerebral Malaria (*Plasmodium falciparum*): The critical tropical mimic of acute encephalitis in endemic areas (Western Kenya, Coast).

qs.q: Which inherited trait is NOT associated with increased resistance to severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria?
qs.e: Several inherited red-cell traits can reduce malaria susceptibility or severity, including sickle cell trait, thalassemias, Duffy negativity for P. vivax, and G6PD deficiency in certain contexts. Cystic fibrosis is not a recognized malaria-protective red-cell trait.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Plasmodium falciparum is the most virulent malaria parasite, causing rapid progression to severe disease and death if untreated. It invades red cells, sequesters in microvasculature, and triggers systemic inflammation.

sections.p: A protozoan parasite transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes. It is responsible for >90% of malaria deaths, especially in sub‑Saharan Africa and low‑resource settings.
b: High parasitemia possible because all life stages develop in blood

sections.p: Ring forms, mature trophozoites, and banana‑shaped gametocytes are seen on smear. Infected RBCs acquire knobs that bind endothelial receptors, causing sequestration.
b: No hypnozoite stage – no liver dormancy

sections.p: Female Anopheles bite injects sporozoites; they travel to liver, multiply, then release merozoites into blood. Some develop into gametocytes for mosquito uptake.
Uncomplicated malaria presents with fever, chills, headache, and anemia. Severe malaria includes cerebral involvement, severe anemia, renal failure, acidosis, and hyperparasitemia.
b: WHO severity criteria: cerebral malaria, >5 % parasitemia, lactate >5 mmol/L, creatinine >265 µmol/L, etc.
Common co‑morbidities: HIV, sickle cell disease, malnutrition

sections.p: Microscopy remains gold standard; rapid diagnostic tests (HRP2) provide bedside confirmation. In low‑resource settings, clinical suspicion guides early treatment.

t.b: Does the patient have malaria parasites? Positive smear confirms species and parasitemia; high % indicates severe disease.
Is P. falciparum present? Positive test is quick but can be false‑negative after HRP2 gene deletions; confirm with smear if possible.
Is there metabolic acidosis? Elevated lactate (>5 mmol/L) signals severe disease and need for intensive care.

sections.p: First‑line therapy uses artemisinin‑based combination therapy (ACT) to clear parasites. Severe disease requires intravenous artesunate plus supportive care.
b: ACT chosen for rapid parasite clearance and low resistance risk
IV artesunate preferred over quinine because of lower mortality and fewer cardiac side‑effects

sections.p: Key points often tested in exams.
b: Sequestration of infected RBCs causes cerebral malaria
HRP2 RDT detects only P. falciparum; negative test does not rule out non‑falciparum species
Severe malaria criteria include >5 % parasitemia or any organ dysfunction

whenToSeekHelp: Altered mental status or seizures (cerebral malaria)
Severe anemia (Hb <5 g/dL) or respiratory distress
Renal failure, shock, or persistent vomiting

faq.q: Why does P. falciparum cause cerebral malaria?
faq.a: Infected RBCs adhere to cerebral microvasculature, blocking flow and causing ischemia and inflammation.

faq.q: Can malaria be diagnosed without a microscope?
faq.a: Yes, HRP2 rapid tests give a quick answer, but confirm with smear when possible, especially if the test is negative but suspicion remains.

faq.q: What is the role of sickle cell trait in falciparum malaria?
faq.a: Trait provides partial protection by reducing parasite growth in sickled cells, lowering severe disease risk.

exam: Describe the WHO criteria for severe P. falciparum malaria and explain why each is clinically important.
Explain the mechanism of microvascular sequestration and its consequences in cerebral malaria.
Compare artemisinin‑based combination therapy with quinine for severe malaria, including reasons for preferring ACT.
